timeline_events.summary: A secret Foreign Office letter warns Downing Street that the Iraq war was fuelling Muslim extremism in Britain, a year before the 7 July bombings.

The US Iraq Survey Group concludes its hunt for Saddam Hussein's alleged weapons of mass destruction and leaves Iraq, with its final report expected to reaffirm the interim finding that Saddam had destroyed his last such weapons more than a decade earlier.
The trial of US Army Specialist Charles Graner, labeled the "primary torturer" at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq, ends abruptly after he declines to testify, with a verdict expected as early as that day.
The British Museum releases a report finding that US-led forces caused substantial damage and severe contamination to the ancient city of Babylon during their use of the site as a military base.
Iraqi authorities take back responsibility for the site of Babylon from coalition forces in a formal handover, inheriting severe and partly irreparable damage caused during the military occupation.
A CIA thinktank report warns that the Iraq war is creating a new generation of "professional" terrorists who will eventually replace al-Qaida as a global threat.

A court martial in Germany hears testimony that British soldiers accused of abusing Iraqi detainees at Camp Bread Basket in Basra in May 2003 were acting under a superior's "Ali Baba" crackdown order, as photographs of the abuse are released.
A British Territorial Army soldier, Lance Corporal George Solomou, publicly refuses deployment to Iraq, saying he would rather go to prison than serve in what he calls an illegal war.
Iraqi trade union leader Hadi Saleh, international secretary of the Iraqi Federation of Trade Unions, was murdered after being tortured by a gang who broke into his Baghdad home.
The US army plans to deploy 18 armed robots, called Swords, to Iraq from March or April to help fight the "war on terror."
A US CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopter crashes in the desert near Rutba in western Iraq, killing 31 US marines in the deadliest single incident for US forces since the Iraq war began.

The article discusses the upcoming Iraqi elections that will ratify and lend constitutional legitimacy to a transformation toward Shia political dominance in Iraq, a prospect that deeply troubles Arab regimes.
Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.

A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.

New evidence emerges that US forces in Afghanistan engaged in widespread Abu Ghraib-style abuse, including sexual humiliation and rape of detainees, and that US soldiers covered up abuse in Afghanistan and in Iraq even after the Abu Ghraib scandal.
In a Brussels speech aimed at mending transatlantic ties after the Iraq war, US President George Bush calls on the EU to support Iraq's new democracy and urges Syria to end its occupation of Lebanon.

The Guardian reports that Attorney General Lord Goldsmith warned less than two weeks before the invasion of Iraq that military action could be ruled illegal, and that a parliamentary answer presented as his official opinion was drawn up in Downing Street rather than his chambers.
The full version of Attorney General Lord Goldsmith's legal opinion on the legality of the Iraq war is discussed as a defining controversy of Tony Blair's premiership, compared to the Suez crisis.
The US military death toll in Iraq since the March 2003 invasion surpassed 1,500, with three soldiers killed in two separate attacks the previous day.
US forces agree to hand over control of the Abu Ghraib prison and other detention facilities to the newly elected Iraqi authorities, though no deadline has been set.

Public health experts from six countries criticize the British and American governments for failing to investigate civilian deaths in the Iraq conflict, calling their reliance on limited Iraqi health ministry data unacceptable.
Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi announces that Italy will begin withdrawing its troops from Iraq in September under domestic pressure.
The British government attempts to suppress evidence that the attorney general believed the war against Iraq was illegal less than two weeks before British troops joined the US-led invasion.

The Conservatives select former RAF Group Captain Al Lockwood, who served as the official military spokesman during the Iraq war, to stand against Tony Blair in his Sedgefield constituency at the forthcoming general election.

A Guardian article by Tariq Ali criticizes the US- and UK-led occupation of Iraq, citing claims that more than 100,000 Iraqi civilians died, and urges tactical anti-war voting in the upcoming British general election.

A memo revealed that the highest-ranking US general in Iraq, Lieutenant General Ricardo Sanchez, authorized interrogation techniques including sleep manipulation, stress positions, and the use of dogs to exploit Arab fears, with 12 techniques exceeding army field manual limits and four risking violation of international law.
A UN expert reports that acute malnutrition among Iraqi children under five nearly doubled in 2004, attributing it to chaos caused by the US-led occupation.

Human rights groups criticize Blackwater Security after a memo to staff in Iraq claimed it is "fun" to shoot people, raising fresh concerns over the role and regulation of civilian contractors operating in Iraq.

A US presidential commission report reveals that Curveball, an Iraqi defector described as "crazy" and a "congenital liar," was the key source behind false pre-war US intelligence claims about Iraq's biological weapons programs.
Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

Two years after US troops took Baghdad, residents and city authorities begin beautification efforts to restore the Iraqi capital, including planting trees, restoring Jadriya lake, and reopening it as a public park.

The UK Ministry of Defence reveals that the number of soldiers deserting or going absent without leave more than doubled over the past year, a rise that coincided with the invasion of Iraq and its aftermath.
Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.

Former UN chief weapons inspector Hans Blix says his inspectors found no compelling evidence that Iraq had a hidden arsenal or was blocking inspections, undercutting a main ground in Lord Goldsmith's legal advice to Tony Blair for the Iraq war.

Leaked documents and disclosures suggest that Lord Goldsmith's full legal advice to Tony Blair on the Iraq war was more ambiguous than his published summary, indicating he changed his advice twice before the war.
A US military jury imposes the death penalty on Sergeant Hasan Akbar, a Muslim US soldier, for a fatal grenade and rifle attack on fellow soldiers in Kuwait in 2003 before the invasion of Iraq.
The US is considering officially allowing women to serve on the front line in Iraq, as the ground war has made the ban unworkable and 35 US servicewomen have died in Iraq.

A Coldstream Guardsman is killed and another injured by a roadside bomb during a night patrol near Amara in southern Iraq, while four car bombs kill 14 people in Baghdad on the eve of the Iraqi government cabinet's swearing-in.

A wounded British soldier who served in Iraq says he will vote against Tony Blair in his Sedgefield constituency and calls for troops to be brought home, citing the war’s dubious legality and his treatment by the army.
Five separate suicide attacks occur across Iraq, killing 71 people and injuring scores more.
Photographs of Saddam Hussein in his underwear are leaked to and published by the Sun newspaper, prompting George Bush to support an investigation into how they entered the public domain.

US Republican congressman Walter Jones, who led the campaign to rename french fries as "freedom fries" in the run-up to the Iraq invasion, says he now opposes the war and wishes the name change had never happened.
Iraq's religious leaders intensify efforts to heal Sunni-Shia rifts through face-to-face talks mediated by Muqtada al-Sadr amid sectarian killings that have raised fears of civil war.

Basra declares itself open to foreign visitors, instructing them to be vigilant, dress like locals, and hire armed escorts, while Iraqi Airways plans regular commercial flights between Basra and Heathrow.
American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.
A CIA report concludes that the war in Iraq is creating a new breed of Islamic jihadists who could destabilize other countries, potentially worse than Afghanistan.

US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns that the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms that the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders in an attempt to quell the violence.

President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.

The Observer reports evidence of secret torture chambers, extra-judicial executions, and a "ghost" network of unaccountable detention facilities run by forces linked to Iraq's Ministry of the Interior.

The article argues that the Iraq war increased the terrorist threat and that the London bombings should be compared to the suffering caused in Iraq, while noting that Tony Blair is partly responsible for the 100,000 people killed in Iraq.
A commentator argues that the London bombings are linked to Britain's role in Iraq and Afghanistan, criticizing the official refusal to discuss those connections.

US media report that White House adviser Karl Rove told a grand jury he discussed the identity of outed CIA operative Valerie Wilson, whose husband Joseph Wilson was an Iraq war critic, with journalists.
A group called Abu Hafs al Masri Brigades, an al-Qaida-linked group, threatens to launch "a bloody war" on the capitals of European countries that do not remove their troops from Iraq within a month.

Al-Qaida's second-in-command Ayman al-Zawahiri warns in a video aired by al-Jazeera that the US faces worse casualties in Iraq than in Vietnam and that Britons will face more destruction unless troops withdraw from Iraq.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

A prominent group of Iraqi women who backed the US-British invasion met the American ambassador to pressure politicians drafting Iraq's constitution not to limit women's rights, amid fears that enshrining Islamic law as a main source of legislation would restrict rights in marriage, divorce and inheritance.
The mood in America is shifting against the Iraq war, but it has found inadequate expression in Congress.

A leaked Iraqi Board of Supreme Audit report concludes that at least half of $1.27 billion in Iraqi funds spent on military procurement disappeared through kickbacks and vanished middlemen or was spent on useless equipment, leading to the firing of nine ministry officials appointed by the US.
A Guardian report reveals that the Iraqi town of Haditha is fully controlled by insurgents, who run security, administration, and communications as a Taliban-like state under the noses of US forces.
The United States eases its opposition to an Islamic Iraqi state to help clinch a deal on a draft constitution before tonight's deadline.

Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

Thousands of pro- and anti-war activists converge near President George Bush's ranch in Crawford, Texas, for dueling rallies, with Cindy Sheehan leading the anti-war protest and conservative groups including the "You Don't Speak for Me, Cindy!" tour staging a counter-rally.

US troops in Baghdad shot dead Reuters soundman Waleed Khaled and detained cameraman Haider Kadhem, an incident cited as evidence that American forces are out of control in their treatment of journalists in Iraq.
The transitional assembly in Iraq signed a constitution amid Sunni rejection and warnings that the unresolved federalism disputes could lead to civil war in the October referendum.
Bulgaria's new government says it will withdraw all its 370 troops from Iraq.
A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.

UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan expresses regret that the UN ever became involved in the Iraq oil-for-food program, saying he wishes the organization had never been given the program, ahead of the publication of an investigation expected to criticize his management.

A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.
Anti-war demonstrators march in central London on the eve of the Labour Party conference to demand the withdrawal of all British troops from Iraq.

British Defense Secretary John Reid expresses confidence that a major withdrawal of British troops from Iraq will begin in May, contingent on the continuing political process, with detailed disengagement plans to be published the following month.
Human Rights Watch issues a report accusing insurgent groups in Iraq of war crimes for deliberately targeting and killing civilians.
George Bush claims he was on a mission from God when he launched the invasion of Iraq, according to Palestinian politician Nabil Shaath.
A senior White House official denies that US President George Bush said God ordered him to invade Afghanistan and Iraq, calling the claims "absurd."

Former Abu Ghraib commander Janis Karpinski publishes a memoir in which she claims she was made a scapegoat for the prison abuse scandal and describes how interrogators enlisted military police in abusive techniques.
A Sunni insurgent leader, Abu Theeb, defies al-Qaida in Iraq by actively supporting the constitutional referendum and securing safe voting for his people, revealing a growing split in the insurgency.

Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, speaking at a UN Food and Agriculture Organisation ceremony in Rome, denounces Tony Blair and George Bush as "international terrorists" and likens their alliance over the Iraq war to Hitler and Mussolini's Axis.
Former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.

A bill proposed by former cabinet minister Clare Short to require parliamentary approval before sending British troops to war, introduced in the wake of the Iraq war, is talked out in the Commons and stands no chance of becoming law.

A US Senate investigation led by Republican Norm Coleman alleges that MP George Galloway lied under oath about receiving oil allocations from Saddam Hussein's Iraqi government under the oil-for-food program, allegations Galloway angrily denies.
US marines conducted Operation Steel Curtain, an offensive against insurgents in north-western Iraq near the Syrian border.
Former British ambassador Sir Christopher Meyer publishes a damning verdict claiming Tony Blair failed to exert leverage on George Bush over the Iraq war and was seduced by US power.
The US government appears to admit that white phosphorus was used in Falluja as a chemical weapon, after previously maintaining it was used only for illumination.

Sajida al-Rishawi, an Iraqi woman, confesses on Jordanian television to her failed suicide bombing attempt at an Amman hotel, part of the November 9 triple hotel attacks carried out by Iraqis from Anbar province that killed 57 people.
Reports reveal that the US used white phosphorus and thermobaric weapons during its assault on Falluja, Iraq, where up to 50,000 civilians remained.
The US military completes Operation Steel Curtain, an offensive against insurgents in towns along Iraq's border with Syria.
An Oxford Research Group report concludes the Iraq war could last decades and that coalition policymakers are being over-optimistic about an exit strategy.

An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.

Former Iraqi Prime Minister Ayad Allawi states that human rights abuses in Iraq under the new government are as bad as or worse than under Saddam Hussein, accusing Shia officials of running death squads and secret torture centers.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.
Two suicide bombers attack a police academy classroom in east Baghdad, killing at least 43 people and injuring 73, with al-Qaida in Iraq claiming responsibility.

US President George Bush admits that much of the intelligence used as the basis for invading Iraq was wrong, but defends his decision to go to war because it removed Saddam Hussein, and pledges that US troops will remain in Iraq until victory is achieved.

The article discusses the ongoing debate over whether the US is an empire and how the Iraq war has revived historical and political discussions about imperialism, noting that this week's elections keep open the prospect that Iraq might ultimately be regarded as a success.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.
Pope John Paul II publicly rebuked President Bush over the invasion of Iraq.

facts.text: On 2005-01-30, Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.
On 2005-03-31, a UN expert reports that acute malnutrition among Iraqi children under five nearly doubled in 2004, attributing it to chaos caused by the US-led occupation.
On 2005-04-06, the Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

On 2005-04-28, former UN chief weapons inspector Hans Blix says his inspectors found no compelling evidence that Iraq had a hidden arsenal or was blocking inspections, undercutting a main ground in Lord Goldsmith's legal advice to Tony Blair for the Iraq war.
On 2005-08-30, Iraq's transitional assembly signed a constitution amid Sunni rejection and warnings that unresolved federalism disputes could lead to civil war in the October referendum.

On 2005-10-17, Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, speaking at a UN Food and Agriculture Organisation ceremony in Rome, denounces Tony Blair and George Bush as "international terrorists" and likens their alliance over the Iraq war to Hitler and Mussolini's Axis.
On 2005-10-19, former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.
On 2005-12-14, US President George Bush admits much of the intelligence used as the basis for invading Iraq was wrong, but defends the war and pledges US troops will remain until victory.

event-1b237c2268b46645.summary: Photographs of Saddam Hussein in his underwear are leaked to and published by the Sun newspaper, prompting George Bush to support an investigation into how they entered the public domain.

event-d6aa69a1c386356d.summary: US Republican congressman Walter Jones, who led the campaign to rename french fries as "freedom fries" in the run-up to the Iraq invasion, says he now opposes the war and wishes the name change had never happened.

event-4da6b32fc0ef8b56.summary: Iraq's religious leaders intensify efforts to heal Sunni-Shia rifts through face-to-face talks mediated by Muqtada al-Sadr amid sectarian killings that have raised fears of civil war.

event-22267fbdfa783fc1.summary: Basra declares itself open to foreign visitors, instructing them to be vigilant, dress like locals, and hire armed escorts, while Iraqi Airways plans regular commercial flights between Basra and Heathrow.

event-aad8eb8935f150b0.summary: American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.

event-70080657c9d30c79.summary: A CIA report concludes that the war in Iraq is creating a new breed of Islamic jihadists who could destabilize other countries, potentially worse than Afghanistan.

event-1111c90fcc1af4d2.summary: US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns that the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms that the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders in an attempt to quell the violence.

event-c99a101acfb8bc69.summary: President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.

event-786b27aadf76c24d.summary: President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

event-564a472abd45b207.summary: Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.

event-c8a6aec6ad411195.summary: The Observer reports evidence of secret torture chambers, extra-judicial executions, and a "ghost" network of unaccountable detention facilities run by forces linked to Iraq's Ministry of the Interior.

event-c1396c061c00a4b8.summary: The article argues that the Iraq war increased the terrorist threat and that the London bombings should be compared to the suffering caused in Iraq, while noting that Tony Blair is partly responsible for the 100,000 people killed in Iraq.

event-8a4ddf649a186212.summary: A commentator argues that the London bombings are linked to Britain's role in Iraq and Afghanistan, criticizing the official refusal to discuss those connections.

event-fbf89c528ae5172f.summary: US media report that White House adviser Karl Rove told a grand jury he discussed the identity of outed CIA operative Valerie Wilson, whose husband Joseph Wilson was an Iraq war critic, with journalists.

event-ba0d210e4005d17a.summary: A group called Abu Hafs al Masri Brigades, an al-Qaida-linked group, threatens to launch "a bloody war" on the capitals of European countries that do not remove their troops from Iraq within a month.

event-39ee71cfc343c069.summary: Al-Qaida's second-in-command Ayman al-Zawahiri warns in a video aired by al-Jazeera that the US faces worse casualties in Iraq than in Vietnam and that Britons will face more destruction unless troops withdraw from Iraq.

event-7e071fb4aa1d2022.summary: Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

event-281942cf0694cadb.summary: A prominent group of Iraqi women who backed the US-British invasion met the American ambassador to pressure politicians drafting Iraq's constitution not to limit women's rights, amid fears that enshrining Islamic law as a main source of legislation would restrict rights in marriage, divorce and inheritance.

event-1d2ab0642752e5dd.summary: The mood in America is shifting against the Iraq war, but it has found inadequate expression in Congress.

event-e714768178fdb342.summary: A leaked Iraqi Board of Supreme Audit report concludes that at least half of $1.27 billion in Iraqi funds spent on military procurement disappeared through kickbacks and vanished middlemen or was spent on useless equipment, leading to the firing of nine ministry officials appointed by the US.

event-e85cf3c3fcb6573d.summary: A Guardian report reveals that the Iraqi town of Haditha is fully controlled by insurgents, who run security, administration, and communications as a Taliban-like state under the noses of US forces.

event-f248c8d350ed4faa.summary: The United States eases its opposition to an Islamic Iraqi state to help clinch a deal on a draft constitution before tonight's deadline.

event-edbd050f20637f61.summary: Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

event-750ed0fed4492523.summary: Thousands of pro- and anti-war activists converge near President George Bush's ranch in Crawford, Texas, for dueling rallies, with Cindy Sheehan leading the anti-war protest and conservative groups including the "You Don't Speak for Me, Cindy!" tour staging a counter-rally.

event-3d002125b9d922aa.summary: US troops in Baghdad shot dead Reuters soundman Waleed Khaled and detained cameraman Haider Kadhem, an incident cited as evidence that American forces are out of control in their treatment of journalists in Iraq.

event-bbf5cedd702405b8.summary: The transitional assembly in Iraq signed a constitution amid Sunni rejection and warnings that the unresolved federalism disputes could lead to civil war in the October referendum.

event-41e5fe9b10a0624b.summary: Bulgaria's new government says it will withdraw all its 370 troops from Iraq.

event-94548d1267fdd9db.summary: A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.

event-b6e61fe7553e341f.summary: UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan expresses regret that the UN ever became involved in the Iraq oil-for-food program, saying he wishes the organization had never been given the program, ahead of the publication of an investigation expected to criticize his management.

event-f63ed29b6ec5e0bf.summary: A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.

event-59a95191801ffa4f.summary: Anti-war demonstrators march in central London on the eve of the Labour Party conference to demand the withdrawal of all British troops from Iraq.

event-0f77e3b2da086fb5.summary: British Defense Secretary John Reid expresses confidence that a major withdrawal of British troops from Iraq will begin in May, contingent on the continuing political process, with detailed disengagement plans to be published the following month.

event-4bcf09b0a8516920.summary: Human Rights Watch issues a report accusing insurgent groups in Iraq of war crimes for deliberately targeting and killing civilians.

event-599f2fa9656ba0e3.summary: George Bush claims he was on a mission from God when he launched the invasion of Iraq, according to Palestinian politician Nabil Shaath.

event-6f9baa6946973be8.summary: A senior White House official denies that US President George Bush said God ordered him to invade Afghanistan and Iraq, calling the claims "absurd."

event-3c0aa65f00999717.summary: Former Abu Ghraib commander Janis Karpinski publishes a memoir in which she claims she was made a scapegoat for the prison abuse scandal and describes how interrogators enlisted military police in abusive techniques.

event-3b2f8a8d9694eec7.summary: A Sunni insurgent leader, Abu Theeb, defies al-Qaida in Iraq by actively supporting the constitutional referendum and securing safe voting for his people, revealing a growing split in the insurgency.

event-064075795749fc35.summary: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, speaking at a UN Food and Agriculture Organisation ceremony in Rome, denounces Tony Blair and George Bush as "international terrorists" and likens their alliance over the Iraq war to Hitler and Mussolini's Axis.

event-676e6dd4ae2c2ac0.summary: Former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.

event-e5b2a7d7b801d557.summary: A bill proposed by former cabinet minister Clare Short to require parliamentary approval before sending British troops to war, introduced in the wake of the Iraq war, is talked out in the Commons and stands no chance of becoming law.

event-78d077d7f282d04c.summary: A US Senate investigation led by Republican Norm Coleman alleges that MP George Galloway lied under oath about receiving oil allocations from Saddam Hussein's Iraqi government under the oil-for-food program, allegations Galloway angrily denies.

event-5e82bde49b35780d.summary: US marines conducted Operation Steel Curtain, an offensive against insurgents in north-western Iraq near the Syrian border.

event-c87b9543ec7d5526.summary: Former British ambassador Sir Christopher Meyer publishes a damning verdict claiming Tony Blair failed to exert leverage on George Bush over the Iraq war and was seduced by US power.

event-3e88f463b0765917.summary: The US government appears to admit that white phosphorus was used in Falluja as a chemical weapon, after previously maintaining it was used only for illumination.

event-d833abb3faa75f33.summary: Sajida al-Rishawi, an Iraqi woman, confesses on Jordanian television to her failed suicide bombing attempt at an Amman hotel, part of the November 9 triple hotel attacks carried out by Iraqis from Anbar province that killed 57 people.

event-b4563b630bc0f0f8.summary: Reports reveal that the US used white phosphorus and thermobaric weapons during its assault on Falluja, Iraq, where up to 50,000 civilians remained.

event-0e03929cb67b78fe.summary: The US military completes Operation Steel Curtain, an offensive against insurgents in towns along Iraq's border with Syria.

event-85fe1c19f7ca63dc.summary: An Oxford Research Group report concludes the Iraq war could last decades and that coalition policymakers are being over-optimistic about an exit strategy.

event-cf878b41671e4b0c.summary: An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.

event-60b9fea49b640c57.summary: Former Iraqi Prime Minister Ayad Allawi states that human rights abuses in Iraq under the new government are as bad as or worse than under Saddam Hussein, accusing Shia officials of running death squads and secret torture centers.

event-da392174a2a97eb1.summary: A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

event-854bec0257212e44.summary: Two suicide bombers attack a police academy classroom in east Baghdad, killing at least 43 people and injuring 73, with al-Qaida in Iraq claiming responsibility.

event-67bff8e5d46b7258.summary: US President George Bush admits that much of the intelligence used as the basis for invading Iraq was wrong, but defends his decision to go to war because it removed Saddam Hussein, and pledges that US troops will remain in Iraq until victory is achieved.

event-17415d8584158960.summary: The article discusses the ongoing debate over whether the US is an empire and how the Iraq war has revived historical and political discussions about imperialism, noting that this week's elections keep open the prospect that Iraq might ultimately be regarded as a success.

event-b390740eb5df97f6.summary: Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.

event-b18e63929be255c9.summary: Pope John Paul II publicly rebuked President Bush over the invasion of Iraq.

events.summary: Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

A Guardian article by Tariq Ali criticizes the US- and UK-led occupation of Iraq, citing claims that more than 100,000 Iraqi civilians died, and urges tactical anti-war voting in the upcoming British general election.

A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.

The article discusses the ongoing debate over whether the US is an empire and how the Iraq war has revived historical and political discussions about imperialism, noting that this week's elections keep open the prospect that Iraq might ultimately be regarded as a success.
Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free and exempted those charged with premeditated murder.
Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free and exempted those charged with premeditated murder.

British Defense Secretary John Reid expresses confidence that a major withdrawal of British troops from Iraq will begin in May, contingent on the continuing political process, with detailed disengagement plans to be published the following month.
The Iraq war drama "Over There" premieres on FX, drawing over 4 million viewers and becoming the most-watched show on cable TV.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.

Leaked documents and disclosures suggest that Lord Goldsmith's full legal advice to Tony Blair on the Iraq war was more ambiguous than his published summary, indicating he changed his advice twice before the war.

Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.
The British government attempts to suppress evidence that the attorney general believed the war against Iraq was illegal less than two weeks before British troops joined the US-led invasion.
Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising.

The UK Ministry of Defence reveals that the number of soldiers deserting or going absent without leave more than doubled over the past year, a rise that coincided with the invasion of Iraq and its aftermath.

A British Territorial Army soldier, Lance Corporal George Solomou, publicly refuses deployment to Iraq, saying he would rather go to prison than serve in what he calls an illegal war.

American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.

Former Iraqi Prime Minister Ayad Allawi states that human rights abuses in Iraq under the new government are as bad as or worse than under Saddam Hussein, accusing Shia officials of running death squads and secret torture centers.

US President George Bush admits that much of the intelligence used as the basis for invading Iraq was wrong, but defends his decision to go to war because it removed Saddam Hussein, and pledges that US troops will remain in Iraq until victory is achieved.

events.summary: Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, potentially benefiting more than 1,000 protesters, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free.
Photographs of Saddam Hussein in his underwear are leaked to and published by the Sun newspaper, prompting George Bush to support an investigation into how they entered the public domain.

The US Iraq Survey Group concludes its hunt for Saddam Hussein's alleged weapons of mass destruction and leaves Iraq, with its final report expected to reaffirm the interim finding that Saddam had destroyed his last such weapons more than a decade earlier.
Former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.

Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.
Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

Leaked documents and disclosures suggest that Lord Goldsmith's full legal advice to Tony Blair on the Iraq war was more ambiguous than his published summary, indicating he changed his advice twice before the war.
A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.
Iraq's religious leaders intensify efforts to heal Sunni-Shia rifts through face-to-face talks mediated by Muqtada al-Sadr amid sectarian killings that have raised fears of civil war.

US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns that the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms that the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders in an attempt to quell the violence.
American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.
A CIA report concludes that the war in Iraq is creating a new breed of Islamic jihadists who could destabilize other countries, potentially worse than Afghanistan.

A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.
A CIA thinktank report warns that the Iraq war is creating a new generation of "professional" terrorists who will eventually replace al-Qaida as a global threat.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

facts.text: On 2005-01-30, Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.
On 2005-04-06, the Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.
On 2005-08-24, Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism.
On 2005-10-19, former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.

On 2005-12-14, US President George Bush admits much of the intelligence used as the basis for invading Iraq was wrong, but defends the decision to go to war and pledges US troops will remain until victory.

On 2005-06-26, US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders to quell the violence.

On 2005-01-13, the US Iraq Survey Group concludes its hunt for Saddam Hussein's alleged weapons of mass destruction and leaves Iraq, its final report expected to reaffirm that Saddam destroyed his last such weapons over a decade earlier.
On 2005-11-23, an Oxford Research Group report concludes the Iraq war could last decades and that coalition policymakers are being over-optimistic about an exit strategy.

events.summary: Two years after US troops took Baghdad, residents and city authorities begin beautification efforts to restore the Iraqi capital, including planting trees, restoring Jadriya lake, and reopening it as a public park.

Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.
Photographs of Saddam Hussein in his underwear are leaked to and published by the Sun newspaper, prompting George Bush to support an investigation into how they entered the public domain.

The US Iraq Survey Group concludes its hunt for Saddam Hussein's alleged weapons of mass destruction and leaves Iraq, with its final report expected to reaffirm the interim finding that Saddam had destroyed his last such weapons more than a decade earlier.
Former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein goes on trial in Baghdad charged with killing 148 people in Dujail following an assassination attempt on him during a visit to the village.
A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.

Leaked documents and disclosures suggest that Lord Goldsmith's full legal advice to Tony Blair on the Iraq war was more ambiguous than his published summary, indicating he changed his advice twice before the war.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.

Basra declares itself open to foreign visitors, instructing them to be vigilant, dress like locals, and hire armed escorts, while Iraqi Airways plans regular commercial flights between Basra and Heathrow.
Iraq's religious leaders intensify efforts to heal Sunni-Shia rifts through face-to-face talks mediated by Muqtada al-Sadr amid sectarian killings that have raised fears of civil war.
Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.
Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.
Iraqi trade union leader Hadi Saleh, international secretary of the Iraqi Federation of Trade Unions, was murdered after being tortured by a gang who broke into his Baghdad home.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, potentially benefiting more than 1,000 protesters, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free.
US forces agree to hand over control of the Abu Ghraib prison and other detention facilities to the newly elected Iraqi authorities, though no deadline has been set.
Iraqi authorities take back responsibility for the site of Babylon from coalition forces in a formal handover, inheriting severe and partly irreparable damage caused during the military occupation.
Five separate suicide attacks occur across Iraq, killing 71 people and injuring scores more.
Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.

A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.

President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.

Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.
A Sunni insurgent leader, Abu Theeb, defies al-Qaida in Iraq by actively supporting the constitutional referendum and securing safe voting for his people, revealing a growing split in the insurgency.
A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.
Five separate suicide attacks occur across Iraq, killing 71 people and injuring scores more.
Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.

The Observer reports evidence of secret torture chambers, extra-judicial executions, and a "ghost" network of unaccountable detention facilities run by forces linked to Iraq's Ministry of the Interior.

An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.

A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.
No topic-related event.

Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.
A Guardian report reveals that the Iraqi town of Haditha is fully controlled by insurgents, who run security, administration, and communications as a Taliban-like state under the noses of US forces.

President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.
A CIA report concludes that the war in Iraq is creating a new breed of Islamic jihadists who could destabilize other countries, potentially worse than Afghanistan.
American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.
A US CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopter crashes in the desert near Rutba in western Iraq, killing 31 US marines in the deadliest single incident for US forces since the Iraq war began.
US forces agree to hand over control of the Abu Ghraib prison and other detention facilities to the newly elected Iraqi authorities, though no deadline has been set.
The United States eases its opposition to an Islamic Iraqi state to help clinch a deal on a draft constitution before tonight's deadline.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

Leading Democrats accuse President George Bush of exploiting the September 11 attacks by linking the Iraq war to the terrorist attacks in his prime-time speech at Fort Bragg, while polls show only a weak boost in support for the war.
No topic-related event.
A senior White House official denies that US President George Bush said God ordered him to invade Afghanistan and Iraq, calling the claims "absurd."
George Bush claims he was on a mission from God when he launched the invasion of Iraq, according to Palestinian politician Nabil Shaath.

Thousands of pro- and anti-war activists converge near President George Bush's ranch in Crawford, Texas, for dueling rallies, with Cindy Sheehan leading the anti-war protest and conservative groups including the "You Don't Speak for Me, Cindy!" tour staging a counter-rally.
The mood in America is shifting against the Iraq war, but it has found inadequate expression in Congress.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, potentially benefiting more than 1,000 protesters, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

events.summary: An Oxford Research Group report concludes the Iraq war could last decades and that coalition policymakers are being over-optimistic about an exit strategy.

British Defense Secretary John Reid expresses confidence that a major withdrawal of British troops from Iraq will begin in May, contingent on the continuing political process, with detailed disengagement plans to be published the following month.
Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi announces that Italy will begin withdrawing its troops from Iraq in September under domestic pressure.

Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.
The British Museum releases a report finding that US-led forces caused substantial damage and severe contamination to the ancient city of Babylon during their use of the site as a military base.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.
The United States eases its opposition to an Islamic Iraqi state to help clinch a deal on a draft constitution before tonight's deadline.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.
The US government appears to admit that white phosphorus was used in Falluja as a chemical weapon, after previously maintaining it was used only for illumination.
A US CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopter crashes in the desert near Rutba in western Iraq, killing 31 US marines in the deadliest single incident for US forces since the Iraq war began.

US troops in Baghdad shot dead Reuters soundman Waleed Khaled and detained cameraman Haider Kadhem, an incident cited as evidence that American forces are out of control in their treatment of journalists in Iraq.

The Conservatives select former RAF Group Captain Al Lockwood, who served as the official military spokesman during the Iraq war, to stand against Tony Blair in his Sedgefield constituency at the forthcoming general election.
Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

A bill proposed by former cabinet minister Clare Short to require parliamentary approval before sending British troops to war, introduced in the wake of the Iraq war, is talked out in the Commons and stands no chance of becoming law.
A commentator argues that the London bombings are linked to Britain's role in Iraq and Afghanistan, criticizing the official refusal to discuss those connections.

Al-Qaida's second-in-command Ayman al-Zawahiri warns in a video aired by al-Jazeera that the US faces worse casualties in Iraq than in Vietnam and that Britons will face more destruction unless troops withdraw from Iraq.

A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.

Former Iraqi Prime Minister Ayad Allawi states that human rights abuses in Iraq under the new government are as bad as or worse than under Saddam Hussein, accusing Shia officials of running death squads and secret torture centers.
A secret Foreign Office letter warns Downing Street that the Iraq war was fuelling Muslim extremism in Britain, a year before the 7 July bombings.
American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, though the vague wording did not immediately free anyone and exempted those charged with premeditated murder.

Human rights groups criticize Blackwater Security after a memo to staff in Iraq claimed it is "fun" to shoot people, raising fresh concerns over the role and regulation of civilian contractors operating in Iraq.
Human Rights Watch issues a report accusing insurgent groups in Iraq of war crimes for deliberately targeting and killing civilians.
The US military completes Operation Steel Curtain, an offensive against insurgents in towns along Iraq's border with Syria.

Public health experts from six countries criticize the British and American governments for failing to investigate civilian deaths in the Iraq conflict, calling their reliance on limited Iraqi health ministry data unacceptable.

A Coldstream Guardsman is killed and another injured by a roadside bomb during a night patrol near Amara in southern Iraq, while four car bombs kill 14 people in Baghdad on the eve of the Iraqi government cabinet's swearing-in.

A suicide bomber detonates 220 kilograms of explosives in al-Uruba Square in the Shia Kadhimiya area of Baghdad, killing 114 people and injuring 150 more, part of one of Iraq's bloodiest days in which 150 people died and 500 were injured.
Reports reveal that the US used white phosphorus and thermobaric weapons during its assault on Falluja, Iraq, where up to 50,000 civilians remained.
Five separate suicide attacks occur across Iraq, killing 71 people and injuring scores more.

events.summary: A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.

Nine people die after insurgents fight a gun battle with Iraqi soldiers and warders at a high-security jail in Baghdad, in an attempt to free prisoners the Iraqi government describes as some of the most dangerous in custody.

Leaked documents and disclosures suggest that Lord Goldsmith's full legal advice to Tony Blair on the Iraq war was more ambiguous than his published summary, indicating he changed his advice twice before the war.

Iraqi politicians negotiate a draft constitution in Baghdad amid extended deadlines, with the draft embracing Islam as a fundamental source of legislation and raising Sunni fears of federalism and potential civil war.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free and exempted those charged with premeditated murder.

US troops in Baghdad shot dead Reuters soundman Waleed Khaled and detained cameraman Haider Kadhem, an incident cited as evidence that American forces are out of control in their treatment of journalists in Iraq.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, potentially benefiting more than 1,000 protesters, though the vague wording did not immediately set anyone free.

An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.
A CIA thinktank report warns that the Iraq war is creating a new generation of "professional" terrorists who will eventually replace al-Qaida as a global threat.
A Sunni insurgent leader, Abu Theeb, defies al-Qaida in Iraq by actively supporting the constitutional referendum and securing safe voting for his people, revealing a growing split in the insurgency.
A US CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopter crashes in the desert near Rutba in western Iraq, killing 31 US marines in the deadliest single incident for US forces since the Iraq war began.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

Former Iraqi Prime Minister Ayad Allawi states that human rights abuses in Iraq under the new government are as bad as or worse than under Saddam Hussein, accusing Shia officials of running death squads and secret torture centers.
US forces agree to hand over control of the Abu Ghraib prison and other detention facilities to the newly elected Iraqi authorities, though no deadline has been set.

Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising, though the vague wording did not immediately free anyone and excluded those charged with premeditated murder.

A prominent group of Iraqi women who backed the US-British invasion met the American ambassador to pressure politicians drafting Iraq's constitution not to limit women's rights, amid fears that enshrining Islamic law as a main source of legislation would restrict rights in marriage, divorce and inheritance.

The US Iraq Survey Group concludes its hunt for Saddam Hussein's alleged weapons of mass destruction and leaves Iraq, with its final report expected to reaffirm the interim finding that Saddam had destroyed his last such weapons more than a decade earlier.
Iraqi parliament elects Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani as president, ending a two-month political deadlock over the make-up of Iraq's new leadership.

A leaked Iraqi Board of Supreme Audit report concludes that at least half of $1.27 billion in Iraqi funds spent on military procurement disappeared through kickbacks and vanished middlemen or was spent on useless equipment, leading to the firing of nine ministry officials appointed by the US.

British Defense Secretary John Reid expresses confidence that a major withdrawal of British troops from Iraq will begin in May, contingent on the continuing political process, with detailed disengagement plans to be published the following month.
American diplomats and army commanders have held indirect talks with insurgents in Iraq, the first officially sanctioned contact between the two sides in two years of violence.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.
Iraq's religious leaders intensify efforts to heal Sunni-Shia rifts through face-to-face talks mediated by Muqtada al-Sadr amid sectarian killings that have raised fears of civil war.
Iraq holds elections under US-led occupation, with disputed turnout figures and widespread Iraqi opposition to the occupation.
Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.
Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi issued a decree pardoning all those charged with or convicted of acts in support of the revolution since the 2011 uprising.

President George W. Bush delivers a televised address from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, linking the Iraq war to the September 11 attacks and outlining a two-track strategy for victory, as a suicide bomber assassinates Iraq's oldest MP, Dhari al-Fayadh, in Baghdad.

US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns that the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms that the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders in an attempt to quell the violence.

A roadside bomb kills three Iraqi National Guards in Baqouba, two Baghdad police are shot dead, an oil pipeline is detonated near Kirkuk, and a mortar attack in Samarra kills a woman and child, as newly elected politicians attempt to form a power-sharing coalition following the January 30 election results.
Five separate suicide attacks occur across Iraq, killing 71 people and injuring scores more.
Iraq's new rulers split over whether to execute Saddam Hussein if convicted of war crimes, with President Jalal Talabani facing calls to resign if he refuses to sign a death warrant.
A Sunni insurgent leader, Abu Theeb, defies al-Qaida in Iraq by actively supporting the constitutional referendum and securing safe voting for his people, revealing a growing split in the insurgency.
A Sunni Arab teenager who drowned saving Shia pilgrims during last week's Baghdad stampede is hailed as a hero whose sacrifice should unify Iraq.

An international journalists group demands complete disclosure from the British and American governments over reports that the US considered bombing al-Jazeera's headquarters, amid concerns that an attack on the broadcaster's Baghdad offices during the Iraq war was deliberate.

Shia leaders in Iraq, led by SCIRI head Abdul Aziz al-Hakim, demand an autonomous region for the Shia-dominated south in the new national constitution, raising the prospect of an oil-rich federal state and drawing fierce opposition from Sunnis and the Shia prime minister.

A prominent military historian calls for President Bush's impeachment over the Iraq war, describing it as the most foolish war since 9 BC and warning that a US troop withdrawal would likely lead Iraq into an all-out civil war.

The British Museum releases a report finding that US-led forces caused substantial damage and severe contamination to the ancient city of Babylon during their use of the site as a military base.

President George Bush delivers a speech at Fort Bragg stating that Iraq is the latest battlefield in the war on terror and that the U.S. mission is to hunt down terrorists and help Iraqis build a free nation.

US troops in Baghdad shot dead Reuters soundman Waleed Khaled and detained cameraman Haider Kadhem, an incident cited as evidence that American forces are out of control in their treatment of journalists in Iraq.

US Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warns that the insurgency in Iraq could continue for at least a decade and confirms that the US army has been in contact with some insurgent leaders in an attempt to quell the violence.
